question:
A 87-year-old male patient visits his PCP reporting a four-month history of symptoms including
intermittent dysuria, ejaculatory pain, mild lower abdominal discomfort, and voiding difficulties. He
denies stool changes or weight loss, and has no family history of cancer. His medical history includes
hypertension and irritable bowel syndrome. Physical examination reveals a well-appearing but slightly
uncomfortable patient. The rectal exam shows no masses, and his prostate, while tender to palpation,
has normal size, texture, and contour. Urinalysis shows trace leukocyte esterase, negative nitrite, no
blood, and no bacteria under microscopy. What is the most appropriate therapeutic approach? Answer
Choices: (A) Tamsulosin and ciprofloxacin (B) Dutasteride (C) Ciprofloxacin (D) Alfuzosin and
doxycycline (E) Ibuprofen and pelvic floor exercises (F) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (G) Finasteride
(H) Doxazosin (I) Watchful waiting with NSAIDs (J) Tamsulosin
 A. Finasteride
B. Doxazosin
C. Ciprofloxacin
D. Tamsulosin
E. Watchful waiting with NSAIDs
F. Tamsulosin and ciprofloxacin
G. Ibuprofen and pelvic floor exercises
H. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
I. Dutasteride
J. Alfuzosin and doxycycline
